concepts.name: Continuity and recovery (business continuity, disaster recovery)

paragraphes: One morning, a power cut turns off your whole school. No lights, no computers, no bell.
Still, lessons go on in the yard, with paper and pencils. Meanwhile, technicians fix the power.
Two things happen at the same time: people keep the essential work going, and others repair the damage. In a company, these are two different plans: business continuity and disaster recovery.

decouverte.comme: At school, one team keeps teaching despite the power cut. Another team fixes the power to get back to normal.
decouverte.enVrai: Business continuity (BC) keeps the essential functions running during the crisis. Disaster recovery (DR) puts the systems back in working order. A disaster is a serious event that stops the work, like a fire. The image stops here: a company prepares these plans before the crisis, not during it.

decouverte.question: A ransomware attack locks all the computers of an online shop. Which plan should the shop start?
decouverte.explanation: The official manual says both start together: one keeps the essentials running, the other puts the systems back in order. Each of the other answers forgets half of the work.

decouverte.titre: A hospital and its computer failure
decouverte.texte: The patient records become unreachable. The nurses switch to paper records: that is continuity, because care does not stop. The IT team gets the system working again: that is recovery.

cards.question: Official definition: “business continuity plan (BCP)”
cards.answer: A business continuity plan (BCP) is a methodology and set of protocols that deals with allowing an organization to keep their key business functions running in the event of a crisis; this is sometimes referred to as continuity of operations (COOP).
cards.explanation: A protocol is a series of written steps to follow. Here, the steps keep the essentials running.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”. Learn it word for word.

cards.question: A business continuity plan (BCP) is a methodology and set of protocols that deals with allowing an organization to keep their [[key]] business functions running in the event of a [[crisis]]; this is sometimes referred to as continuity of operations (COOP).
cards.answer: A business continuity plan (BCP) is a methodology and set of protocols that deals with allowing an organization to keep their key business functions running in the event of a crisis; this is sometimes referred to as continuity of operations (COOP).
cards.explanation: We protect the key functions during a crisis.

cards.question: A business continuity plan (BCP) is a [[methodology and set of protocols]] that deals with [[allowing an organization to keep]] their key business functions running [[in the event of a crisis]]; this is sometimes referred to as continuity of operations (COOP).
cards.answer: A business continuity plan (BCP) is a methodology and set of protocols that deals with allowing an organization to keep their key business functions running in the event of a crisis; this is sometimes referred to as continuity of operations (COOP).
cards.explanation: Three blocks: a written method, the goal (keep the functions running), and the moment (in a crisis).

cards.question: Write the official definition of the “business continuity plan (BCP)” from memory (in English).
cards.answer: A business continuity plan (BCP) is a methodology and set of protocols that deals with allowing an organization to keep their key business functions running in the event of a crisis; this is sometimes referred to as continuity of operations (COOP).
cards.explanation: Think of the school during the power cut: lessons go on. Compare, spot what is missing, try again tomorrow.

cards.question: Official definition: “disaster recovery plan (DRP)”
cards.answer: A disaster recovery plan (DRP) is the set of processes that deal with restoring your information systems and operations, securely and efficiently, after a disruptive event occurs.
cards.explanation: Think of the technical team that repairs: it puts everything back in order after the failure.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”. Learn it word for word.

cards.question: A disaster recovery plan (DRP) is the set of [[processes]] that deal with [[restoring]] your information systems and operations, securely and efficiently, after a disruptive event occurs.
cards.answer: A disaster recovery plan (DRP) is the set of processes that deal with restoring your information systems and operations, securely and efficiently, after a disruptive event occurs.
cards.explanation: Processes to restore, which means to put back in working order.

cards.question: A disaster recovery plan (DRP) is [[the set of processes]] that deal with [[restoring your information systems and operations]], securely and efficiently, [[after a disruptive event occurs]].
cards.answer: A disaster recovery plan (DRP) is the set of processes that deal with restoring your information systems and operations, securely and efficiently, after a disruptive event occurs.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: processes, what we put back in order (systems and operations), and when (after the event).

cards.question: Write the official definition of the “disaster recovery plan (DRP)” from memory (in English).
cards.answer: A disaster recovery plan (DRP) is the set of processes that deal with restoring your information systems and operations, securely and efficiently, after a disruptive event occurs.
cards.explanation: Remember the two adverbs: securely and efficiently. They mean in a safe and effective way.

cards.question: Official definition: “DR” compared with “BC”
cards.answer: DR is the subset of BC whose primary objective is to minimize business downtime and reclaim normal operations as soon as possible.
cards.explanation: Recovery is one part of continuity: the part that brings everything back to normal.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”. “Downtime” means the time when work is stopped.

cards.question: DR is the [[subset of BC]] whose primary objective is to [[minimize business downtime]] and [[reclaim normal operations]] as soon as possible.
cards.answer: DR is the subset of BC whose primary objective is to minimize business downtime and reclaim normal operations as soon as possible.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: a part of continuity, which shortens the stoppage, and which gets back to normal.

cards.question: During a flood, some employees work from home while the technical team gets the server running again. Working from home is part of:
cards.answer: Business continuity (BC)
cards.explanation: Working from home keeps the business running. Getting the server running again is recovery.

cards.question: A fire destroys a company's office. Which of these actions is part of disaster recovery (DR)?
options: Moving the employees to a temporary office
Telling customers that orders now go through the phone
Delivering to customers from another warehouse
options_why: It lets people work during the crisis: that is continuity.
It keeps the business running during the crisis: that is continuity.
It keeps the essential part of the business running: that is continuity.
cards.answer: Repairing the destroyed computer systems
cards.explanation: Recovery takes care of putting the systems and the data back in order.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1. The manual lists shelter, for example another place to work, among the needs of people in the continuity plan.

cards.question: What does COOP mean?
cards.answer: Continuity of operations: another name for the business continuity plan (BCP).
cards.explanation: Two names for the same idea: keeping the operations running.

cards.question: Why do continuity and recovery start at the same time during a disaster?
cards.answer: Because the company must keep its essentials running while the repairs happen. Waiting for the repairs to end would stop the business for too long.
cards.explanation: One protects the business during the crisis, the other brings it back to normal. Both are needed right away.

cards.question: The disaster recovery plan (DRP) focuses on [[systems]], applications, and [[data]].
cards.answer: The disaster recovery plan (DRP) focuses on systems, applications, and data.
cards.explanation: An application is a program. Recovery mostly aims at the technology, not the whole company.

cards.question: Which box does each action go in?
cards.answer: Continuity (BC): manual cash register, temporary office, informing customers. Recovery (DR): restore the server, repair the network, reinstall the applications.
cards.explanation: Ask yourself: does the action keep the business running (BC), or put the technology back in order (DR)?

items.text: The cashiers switch to a manual cash register
The employees work in a temporary office
We tell all the customers about the situation
Restore the orders server from a backup
Repair the destroyed network
Reinstall the lost applications

cards.question: What if a company had only a recovery plan, without a continuity plan?
cards.answer: It would know how to repair its systems, but nobody would know what to do in the meantime. The essential work would stop during the whole repair.
cards.explanation: Recovery brings things back to normal, but it takes time. You need a plan to hold on during that time.

cards.question: Name two types of crises that a continuity plan covers.
cards.answer: Attacks, like ransomware or a distributed denial of service (DDoS: launched from many computers at once). Or natural disasters that stop a data center (a big room full of servers).
cards.explanation: The continuity plan covers all crises, from a computer attack to a natural disaster.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, note on BCP and DRP.

cards.question: Which plan covers all the important functions of the company, not only the IT?
cards.answer: The continuity plan (BCP)
cards.explanation: The BCP is broad: all the critical functions. The DRP is narrower: systems, applications, and data.

cards.question: A hacker blocks the website of an online bookshop. Give one example of a continuity action and one example of a recovery action.
cards.answer: Continuity: take orders by phone during the failure. Recovery: restore the website from a backup and put the servers back in working order.
cards.explanation: Continuity keeps sales possible. Recovery gets the website running again.

cards.question: According to the manual, business continuity includes preventive measures (taken before the problem) and what else?
cards.answer: The management of employees: everything that helps the company stay in working order during a disaster.
cards.explanation: Preventive measures come on top of how people are managed during the crisis.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, definition of the BCP.

concepts.name: The impact analysis (business impact analysis, BIA)

decouverte.titre: The truck that is too small
paragraphes: You are moving house, but the truck is small. Not everything will fit in the first trip.
You sort your things: the bed and the fridge first, the boxes of decorations later. For each object, you ask yourself what happens if you do not have it tonight.
A company does the same thing before a crisis. This exercise is called the business impact analysis (BIA).

decouverte.comme: For each object, you note how much you need it. Without the bed, you sleep badly. Without the decoration boxes, nobody notices.
decouverte.enVrai: The company lists its critical business functions (CBF): the ones without which the business really stops. For each one, it measures what an interruption would cost. Then it decides what to protect first. The image stops here: in a company, several people decide together.

decouverte.question: Who should help find the critical functions of a company?
options: A group: system owners, experts, customers, and suppliers
decouverte.answer: A group: system owners, experts, customers, and suppliers
decouverte.explanation: Each person sees the company from a different angle. The IT team does not see everything, and neither does the director.

decouverte.texte: A pizzeria lists what it needs. The cooks: the staff. Taking orders: a process. The cash register software: a system. The oven: another asset, which means an object of value for the company. Without the oven, no pizzas: it is critical. The monthly newsletter is not.

cards.question: Official definition: “business impact analysis (BIA)”
cards.answer: According to the ISO, a business impact analysis is "the process of analyzing the impact over time of a disruption on the organization."
cards.explanation: Think of the move: we look at what each loss costs, and for how long.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”. The ISO is the International Organization for Standardization. Learn it word for word.

cards.question: According to the ISO, a business impact analysis is "the [[process]] of analyzing the [[impact]] over time of a disruption on the organization."
cards.answer: According to the ISO, a business impact analysis is "the process of analyzing the impact over time of a disruption on the organization."
cards.explanation: A process that analyzes the impact: this is the heart of the BIA.

cards.question: According to the ISO, a business impact analysis is "the [[process of analyzing]] the [[impact over time]] of [[a disruption on the organization]]."
cards.answer: According to the ISO, a business impact analysis is "the process of analyzing the impact over time of a disruption on the organization."
cards.explanation: Three blocks: analyzing, the impact over time, of a disruption on the organization.

cards.question: Write the official definition of the “business impact analysis” according to the ISO from memory (in English).
cards.answer: According to the ISO, a business impact analysis is "the process of analyzing the impact over time of a disruption on the organization."
cards.explanation: The three important words: process, impact over time, disruption.

cards.question: Official definition: what the “BIA” is for
cards.answer: In other words, a BIA helps an organization identify its essential business functions and understand the impact that a disaster would have on each of those functions; the BIA provides the primary justification for the business continuity plan and its requirements.
cards.explanation: The BIA explains why we need the plan: it shows what is at stake.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”.

cards.question: In other words, a BIA helps an organization [[identify its essential business functions]] and [[understand the impact]] that a disaster would have on each of those functions; the BIA provides [[the primary justification]] for the business continuity plan and its requirements.
cards.answer: In other words, a BIA helps an organization identify its essential business functions and understand the impact that a disaster would have on each of those functions; the BIA provides the primary justification for the business continuity plan and its requirements.
cards.explanation: Two roles: find the essential functions and their impact, then justify the plan.

cards.question: In which family of critical functions does each item belong?
cards.answer: Personnel: the nurses. Processes: taking orders by phone, billing. Systems: the payroll software, the booking server. Other assets: the delivery truck.
cards.explanation: The manual lists four families: personnel, processes, systems and applications, and other assets.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: “Personnel, Business processes, Information systems and applications, Other assets”.

items.text: The nurses of a hospital
Taking orders by phone
The way billing is done each month
The payroll software
The booking server
The delivery truck

cards.question: Which document explains why the company needs a continuity plan?
cards.answer: The impact analysis (BIA)
cards.explanation: The BIA shows what is at stake. The BCP is the answer built from it.

cards.question: What does CBF mean?
cards.answer: Critical business function: a function of the company without which its business is really threatened.
cards.explanation: The key word is business: we look for what is vital for the company's activity.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section on the BIA.

cards.question: Why do we need the opinion of customers and suppliers to find the critical functions?
cards.answer: Each person sees the company from a different angle. A customer immediately sees the service they cannot do without.
cards.explanation: One person easily forgets some functions. Several points of view give a more complete list.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: system owners, experts, customers, and suppliers help find the critical functions.

cards.question: Critical functions include the [[personnel]], the processes, the systems, and the other [[assets]].
cards.answer: Critical functions include the personnel, the processes, the systems, and the other assets.
cards.explanation: Four families: the people, the ways of working, the IT, and everything else.

cards.question: What if a company skips the impact analysis and protects everything in the same way?
cards.answer: It spends too much on unimportant functions, and not enough on the ones that really matter. Without priorities, the budget is badly shared.
cards.explanation: The BIA is used to choose: we protect first what really hurts if we lose it.

cards.question: A company has just listed its critical functions. What should it do next for each one?
options: Look for what could go wrong and how likely it is
Buy new equipment for each one
Remove the ones that earn the least money
Hire extra staff for each one
options_why: We buy nothing before we know what is really threatened.
Critical does not mean profitable: a function can be vital without earning much.
Hiring does not solve the problem as long as we do not know what is threatened.
cards.answer: Look for what could go wrong and how likely it is
cards.explanation: The manual asks for a risk analysis of each function: its weak points, the chance of a problem, and the acceptable impact.

cards.question: Put the steps of the BIA in order.
cards.answer: 1 Form the team and set the scope and the budget. 2 Make sure management supports it. 3 Identify the critical functions. 4 Analyze their weak points and the acceptable impact.
cards.explanation: We prepare first (team, budget, support), then we list the functions, then we analyze each one.

items: Form the project team, set the scope and the budget
Analyze the weak points and the acceptable impact of each one

cards.question: Why is the support of management needed for a continuity plan?
cards.answer: The plan brings nothing visible right away. So management must agree to pay for the money, the staff, and the strategic vision.
cards.explanation: Without support from the top, nobody pays for a danger that has not happened yet.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: “BCP does not yield an immediate or tangible return”.

paragraphes: You are playing online with three friends. In the middle of the game, your console crashes. The screen goes black.
Your friends wait for you for a while. After ten minutes, it feels long. After an hour, they start another game without you and stop inviting you.
So there is a maximum waiting time, and after it the damage becomes lasting. In a company, this is the maximum tolerable downtime (MTD).

decouverte.comme: For a while, your friends accept to wait. Then comes a moment when they leave for good.
decouverte.enVrai: A critical business function (CBF) can stay stopped for some time without much harm. Past the limit, the damage becomes lasting: lost customers, a company in danger. This limit is the MTD. The image stops here: the limit is set by the system owner, the person responsible for the function.

decouverte.question: An online shop is down. What does its MTD represent?
options: The time the technicians expect the repair to take
The maximum time before lasting damage to the company
The length of the last failure
decouverte.answer: The maximum time before lasting damage to the company
decouverte.explanation: The expected repair time is another measure, which you will see in the next planet. The MTD is a limit, not a forecast.

decouverte.texte: A bakery loses its cash register at seven in the morning. Customers wait a little, then go to the neighbor. If the register stays broken for more than two days, many will never come back. These two days are the MTD of this function (an invented example to help you understand).

cards.question: Official definition: “maximum tolerable downtime (MTD)”
cards.answer: Maximum tolerable downtime (MTD), or maximum acceptable outage (MAO), expresses the total length of time a critical business function can be unavailable without causing significant, long-term harm to the business; it is the longest time a CBF can remain disabled before it threatens the organization's long-term survival.
cards.explanation: Think of your friends' patience: past the limit, they leave for good.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”. Learn it word for word.

cards.question: Maximum tolerable downtime (MTD), or maximum acceptable outage (MAO), expresses the total length of time a critical business function can be [[unavailable]] without causing significant, long-term harm to the business; it is the longest time a CBF can remain disabled before it threatens the organization's long-term [[survival]].
cards.answer: Maximum tolerable downtime (MTD), or maximum acceptable outage (MAO), expresses the total length of time a critical business function can be unavailable without causing significant, long-term harm to the business; it is the longest time a CBF can remain disabled before it threatens the organization's long-term survival.
cards.explanation: Two ideas: the function is unavailable, and the company's survival is at stake.

cards.question: Maximum tolerable downtime (MTD), or maximum acceptable outage (MAO), expresses [[the total length of time]] a critical business function can be unavailable [[without causing significant, long-term harm]] to the business; it is [[the longest time a CBF can remain disabled]] before it threatens the organization's long-term survival.
cards.answer: Maximum tolerable downtime (MTD), or maximum acceptable outage (MAO), expresses the total length of time a critical business function can be unavailable without causing significant, long-term harm to the business; it is the longest time a CBF can remain disabled before it threatens the organization's long-term survival.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: a total length of time, without lasting harm, and the longest time stopped.

cards.question: Write the official definition of the “maximum tolerable downtime (MTD)” from memory (in English).
cards.answer: Maximum tolerable downtime (MTD), or maximum acceptable outage (MAO), expresses the total length of time a critical business function can be unavailable without causing significant, long-term harm to the business; it is the longest time a CBF can remain disabled before it threatens the organization's long-term survival.
cards.explanation: It is a long sentence: remember the two halves, before the semicolon and after it.

cards.question: Official definition: who defines the “MTD”
cards.answer: MTD must be defined by the system owner, who is ultimately responsible to the organization for the proper operation of the CBF.
cards.explanation: The person who answers for the function decides how long it can stay stopped.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”.

cards.question: MTD must be defined by [[the system owner]], who is ultimately [[responsible to the organization]] for [[the proper operation of the CBF]].
cards.answer: MTD must be defined by the system owner, who is ultimately responsible to the organization for the proper operation of the CBF.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the system owner, their responsibility to the organization, and the proper working of the function.

cards.question: Official definition: exceeding the “MTD”
cards.answer: Exceeding the MTD is an expression of unacceptable risk by the business owner.
cards.explanation: Exceeding the limit means going beyond what the business owner can accept.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”.

cards.question: [[Exceeding the MTD]] is an expression of [[unacceptable risk]] by [[the business owner]].
cards.answer: Exceeding the MTD is an expression of unacceptable risk by the business owner.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: exceeding the MTD, an unacceptable risk, the business owner.

cards.question: Who sets the MTD of a critical function?
options: The technicians who do the repair
cards.answer: The system owner
cards.explanation: The owner answers for the function to the company: they know what a stoppage that is too long would cost.

cards.question: What is the other name of the MTD?
cards.answer: MAO: maximum acceptable outage.
cards.explanation: Two abbreviations for the same limit: MTD (tolerable downtime) or MAO (acceptable outage).

cards.question: A company thinks that after two days of downtime of its online shop, many customers will leave forever. What do these two days represent?
options: The normal length of a repair
The delay to warn the customers
options_why: A repair lasts as long as it lasts. Here, we talk about a limit that must not be passed.
The time between two backups is about lost data, not the length of the stoppage.
Warning the customers is an action of the plan, not the limit before lasting damage.
cards.answer: Its maximum tolerable downtime (MTD)
cards.explanation: The two days are the limit before lasting damage. This is exactly the definition of the MTD.

cards.question: Why is the MTD set by the system owner and not by the technicians?
cards.answer: The owner answers for the proper working of the function to the company. They know what a stoppage costs, while the technicians mostly see the repair.
cards.explanation: The limit depends on the value of the function for the business, not on how hard the technical work is.

cards.question: The MTD is the [[longest]] downtime before the company's [[survival]] is threatened.
cards.answer: The MTD is the longest downtime before the company's survival is threatened.
cards.explanation: Think of your friends' patience: a maximum, not an average.

cards.question: What if a critical function stays stopped for longer than its MTD?
cards.answer: The damage becomes serious and lasting, and the company's survival is threatened. Passing the MTD is a risk that the company did not want to accept.
cards.explanation: The MTD is the last border before lasting damage.

cards.question: The MTD is more like:
options: A limit that must not be passed
A forecast of the length of the failure
cards.answer: A limit that must not be passed
cards.explanation: A forecast says what we expect. A limit says what we refuse to go beyond. The MTD is a limit.

cards.question: A pizzeria loses its order system. If the stoppage lasts more than four hours on a Saturday night, customers will not come back. What is this limit called, and who sets it?
cards.answer: It is the MTD (maximum tolerable downtime). The system owner sets it, because they are responsible for the proper working of the function.
cards.explanation: Four hours is the limit before lasting damage. It comes from the business, not from the technology.

decouverte.titre: I will be back in ten minutes
paragraphes: Your console crashed. You turn it on again, restart the game, and rejoin your friends. It takes you six minutes.
Your friends ask: “How long until you are back?” You promise: “Ten minutes at most.”
This promise is the recovery time objective (RTO): the time we give ourselves to restart.

decouverte.comme: You do not promise the time that would make you lose your friends. You promise less, to stay well under their patience.
decouverte.enVrai: The RTO is the time the company gives itself to get a function running again. It must stay shorter than the MTD, the limit that must not be passed. If the RTO is too long, the company adds protections (controls) to shorten it.

decouverte.question: How does the RTO of a function compare with its MTD?
options: Shorter than or equal to the MTD
Nothing to do with the MTD
decouverte.answer: Shorter than or equal to the MTD
decouverte.explanation: If the restart took longer than the limit before lasting damage, the damage would already be done.

decouverte.texte: An online shop has an MTD of twenty-four hours. Its team gives itself an RTO of four hours: within four hours, the site must take orders again. This keeps a big margin before the point of no return (invented numbers to help you understand).

cards.question: Official definition: “recovery time objective (RTO)”
cards.answer: Recovery time objective (RTO) is the planned time necessary to restore a system to the point where it meets the minimum service expectations of the system owner.
cards.explanation: Think of your promise: the planned time to be usable again.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”. Learn it word for word.

cards.question: Recovery time objective (RTO) is the [[planned]] time necessary to [[restore]] a system to the point where it meets the minimum service expectations of the system owner.
cards.answer: Recovery time objective (RTO) is the planned time necessary to restore a system to the point where it meets the minimum service expectations of the system owner.
cards.explanation: A time planned in advance, to put the system back in working order.

cards.question: Recovery time objective (RTO) is the planned time necessary to [[restore a system]] to the point where it meets [[the minimum service expectations]] of [[the system owner]].
cards.answer: Recovery time objective (RTO) is the planned time necessary to restore a system to the point where it meets the minimum service expectations of the system owner.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: put the system back in order, the minimum level of service, and the person who expects it.

cards.question: Write the official definition of the “recovery time objective (RTO)” from memory (in English).
cards.answer: Recovery time objective (RTO) is the planned time necessary to restore a system to the point where it meets the minimum service expectations of the system owner.
cards.explanation: Remember: planned time, restore, minimum service expectations.

cards.question: Official definition: the “RTO” seen as a maximum
cards.answer: In other words, RTO is the maximum period of time within which a CBF must be restored after a disruption to avoid unacceptable business consequences.
cards.explanation: It is the same idea, said differently: a maximum delay to start again.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”.

cards.question: In other words, RTO is [[the maximum period of time]] within which a CBF must be [[restored after a disruption]] to avoid [[unacceptable business consequences]].
cards.answer: In other words, RTO is the maximum period of time within which a CBF must be restored after a disruption to avoid unacceptable business consequences.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the maximum period, restoring after the disruption, and avoiding unacceptable consequences.

cards.question: Official definition: the link between the “RTO” and the “MTD”
cards.answer: Since unacceptable disaster occurs when the MTD is exceeded, the RTO, by definition, must be less than or equal to the MTD.
cards.explanation: The RTO must always end before the limit of the MTD.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”.

cards.question: Since [[unacceptable disaster]] occurs when [[the MTD is exceeded]], the RTO, by definition, must be [[less than or equal]] to the MTD.
cards.answer: Since unacceptable disaster occurs when the MTD is exceeded, the RTO, by definition, must be less than or equal to the MTD.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the unacceptable disaster, the MTD exceeded, and the rule RTO less than or equal.

cards.question: The MTD of a function is ten hours. Is an RTO of twelve hours acceptable?
cards.answer: No
cards.explanation: The RTO must be less than or equal to the MTD. Twelve hours is beyond the limit of ten hours.

cards.question: A company plans six hours to get its cash register running again. Its limit before lasting damage is four hours. What should it do?
options: Add measures to bring the RTO under the limit
Keep the plan as it is, it is almost right
Move the limit back to six hours
options_why: Almost is not enough: the RTO must be less than or equal to the MTD.
The limit comes from what the company can bear. We do not move it to suit the plan.
One more backup does not always shorten the recovery time.
cards.answer: Add measures to bring the RTO under the limit
cards.explanation: The manual says the RTO is adjusted by applying extra controls to stay within the MTD.

cards.question: What does RTO mean?
cards.answer: Recovery time objective: the planned time to bring a system back to the minimum level of service.
cards.explanation: Time is in the name: the RTO is about the length of time to start again.

cards.question: Why must the RTO be shorter than the MTD, or equal to it?
cards.answer: The MTD is the limit before lasting damage. If the recovery takes longer than this limit, the damage is already done.
cards.explanation: The RTO is the target, the MTD is the limit that must never be crossed.

cards.question: The RTO must be [[less]] than or equal to the [[MTD]].
cards.answer: The RTO must be less than or equal to the MTD.
cards.explanation: The RTO is used to stay under the limit.

cards.question: What if the planned RTO is too long compared with the MTD?
cards.answer: The company must add protections (controls) to shorten the recovery. If not, it accepts the risk of passing its limit.
cards.explanation: Each extra control costs money. It is a choice of the company.

cards.question: What does it mean when the business owner does not want to add more controls?
cards.answer: They accept the risk: they choose to live with a slower recovery rather than pay more.
cards.explanation: Stopping the addition of controls is a decision, not an oversight.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: “they have accepted the risk of operation”.

cards.question: Put these moments in order on the timeline.
cards.answer: 1 The incident stops the function. 2 The RTO: the function must be running again. 3 The MTD: the limit before lasting damage.
cards.explanation: The RTO comes before the limit. If we pass the MTD, lasting damage begins.

items: The RTO: the function must be running again
The MTD: the limit before lasting damage

cards.question: A hospital sets an MTD of two hours for its patient records. Among 1 h 30, 2 h 30, and 3 h, which RTO is consistent? Explain.
cards.answer: 1 h 30. Only an RTO of two hours or less stays under the limit of the MTD.
cards.explanation: The two other durations go past the MTD, so the lasting damage would already have happened.

paragraphes: Your console crashes. You restart your game. Surprise: your game is there, but you lost the last ten minutes.
The game saved by itself every ten minutes. What happened since the last save has disappeared.
How many minutes of play can you accept to lose? In a company, this limit is called the recovery point objective (RPO).

decouverte.titre: The more you save, the less you lose
decouverte.comme: If the game saves every minute, you lose little when the console crashes. But the console has to work much harder.
decouverte.enVrai: The RPO measures the amount of data we accept to lose, shown as a length of time. An RPO of one hour means: we can lose at most the last hour of work. The shorter the RPO, the more often we must back up. The image stops here: a company loses orders or payments, not only minutes of play.

decouverte.question: A shop saves its orders every 24 hours. It fails at 6 pm. What can it lose at worst?
options: The orders of the last day
decouverte.answer: The orders of the last day
decouverte.explanation: Everything that arrived since the last backup is lost. The less often we back up, the bigger the possible loss.

decouverte.texte: A bank cannot lose a single transaction: its RPO is almost zero. An online bookshop can accept to lose one hour of orders: its RPO is one hour. Each company chooses according to what it cannot afford to lose.

cards.question: Official definition: “recovery point objective (RPO)”
cards.answer: Recovery Point Objective (RPO) represents the measurement of tolerable data loss, represented as a period of time.
cards.explanation: Think of the game save: how many minutes of play you accept to lose.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”. Learn it word for word.

cards.question: Recovery Point Objective (RPO) represents the [[measurement]] of tolerable data [[loss]], represented as a period of time.
cards.answer: Recovery Point Objective (RPO) represents the measurement of tolerable data loss, represented as a period of time.
cards.explanation: A measure of the data loss that we tolerate.

cards.question: Recovery Point Objective (RPO) represents [[the measurement]] of [[tolerable data loss]], represented as [[a period of time]].
cards.answer: Recovery Point Objective (RPO) represents the measurement of tolerable data loss, represented as a period of time.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: a measure, the tolerable data loss, and a length of time.

cards.question: Write the official definition of the “recovery point objective (RPO)” from memory (in English).
cards.answer: Recovery Point Objective (RPO) represents the measurement of tolerable data loss, represented as a period of time.
cards.explanation: Remember the three key words: measurement, tolerable data loss, period of time.

cards.question: Official definition: who defines the “RPO”
cards.answer: As with the MTD, this must be defined by the business, and the business is responsible for resourcing the controls to achieve the RPO.
cards.explanation: The business decides the tolerable loss, and pays to reach it.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”. “Resourcing” means providing the means.

cards.question: As with the MTD, this must be [[defined by the business]], and the business is responsible for [[resourcing the controls]] to [[achieve the RPO]].
cards.answer: As with the MTD, this must be defined by the business, and the business is responsible for resourcing the controls to achieve the RPO.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: defined by the business, which provides the means, to reach the RPO.

cards.question: The RPO mostly measures:
options: The amount of data we accept to lose
cards.answer: The amount of data we accept to lose
cards.explanation: The time to restart is another abbreviation, the RTO. The RPO is about lost data.

cards.question: A company accepts to lose at most one hour of data. How often must it back up, at the very least?
options_why: With one backup a day, we can lose up to twenty-four hours of data.
With one backup a week, the possible loss is a whole week.
With one backup a month, the possible loss is a whole month.
cards.answer: At least every hour
cards.explanation: The maximum loss is the time since the last backup. So we must back up at least as often as the RPO.

cards.question: What does RPO mean?
cards.answer: Recovery point objective: the tolerable data loss, shown as a length of time.
cards.explanation: The point is the moment of the last backup, where we go back to.

cards.question: Why does a very short RPO cost more?
cards.answer: To lose little data, we must back up very often. This needs more storage, more network use, and more work.
cards.explanation: Each extra backup costs resources. The company must provide them.

cards.question: The RPO is shown as a [[duration]]: the amount of work, in time, that we are willing to [[lose]].
cards.answer: The RPO is shown as a duration: the amount of work, in time, that we are willing to lose.
cards.explanation: For example, we say: we can lose at most one hour of data.

cards.question: What if the last backup is five hours old, while the RPO is one hour?
cards.answer: The company would lose more data than it tolerates. It must back up more often to respect the RPO.
cards.explanation: The RPO sets the maximum gap between two backups.

cards.question: Who defines the RPO?
options: The people in charge of the business
cards.answer: The people in charge of the business
cards.explanation: How much data we can lose depends on the business. The technicians provide the means.

cards.question: Sort these RPOs from the shortest to the longest.
cards.answer: No data lost, then at most 15 minutes, then at most 1 hour, then at most 24 hours.
cards.explanation: A short RPO means backing up very often. A long RPO leaves more time between two backups.

items: At most 15 minutes of data lost
At most 1 hour of data lost
At most 24 hours of data lost

cards.question: An online bookshop sets an RPO of two hours. Its last backup is three hours old. What do you say?
cards.answer: It does not respect its RPO: it risks losing three hours of orders while it tolerates only two. It must back up more often.
cards.explanation: Compare the gap since the last backup with the RPO: if it is bigger, it is too much.

cards.question: Who must provide the means to reach the RPO?
cards.answer: The company itself (the business), which is responsible for resourcing the controls to achieve the RPO.
cards.explanation: Setting an RPO without giving the means makes no sense.

paragraphes: Your console crashes. Three questions come to your mind, and each one has its own clock.
When were you last saved? How long to restart? How long will your friends wait for you?
In a company, these three clocks are called the RPO, the RTO, and the MTD. Mixing them up is the most common mistake.

decouverte.comme: You draw a line. In the middle, the crash. On the left, the time since the last save. On the right, the time to restart, then the moment when your friends leave for good.
decouverte.enVrai: To the left of the incident: the RPO, how far back we lost data. To the right: the RTO, the time to restart, then the MTD, the survival limit of the function. The RPO looks backward. The RTO and the MTD look forward.

decouverte.question: A failure happens at noon. The last backup is from nine o'clock. Which duration do these three hours show?
options: The RTO: the time to restart
decouverte.explanation: These three hours are the data lost since the last backup. The RTO and the MTD are counted after the failure.

decouverte.texte: An online pharmacy backs up its prescriptions every hour: an RPO of one hour. It wants to restart within two hours: an RTO of two hours. After twelve hours of downtime, too many customers go elsewhere: an MTD of twelve hours. These choices depend on its risk tolerance: the level of danger it accepts to face (invented numbers).

cards.question: Official definition: “MTD, RTO and RPO”
cards.answer: MTD, RTO, and RPO are essential thresholds for business continuity planning.
cards.explanation: Three thresholds to know: they decide how much the company can lose and how long it can wait.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”. A threshold is a limit.

cards.question: [[MTD, RTO, and RPO]] are [[essential thresholds]] for [[business continuity planning]].
cards.answer: MTD, RTO, and RPO are essential thresholds for business continuity planning.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the three abbreviations, essential thresholds, to plan continuity.

cards.question: Official definition: “MTD, RTO and RPO” and risk
cards.answer: MTD, RTO, and RPO are important planning horizons and estimates that are strongly linked to an organization's risk tolerance.
cards.explanation: These durations depend on the danger that the company accepts to face.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, note after figure 1.4.

cards.question: MTD, RTO, and RPO are [[important planning horizons]] and estimates that are [[strongly linked]] to an organization's [[risk tolerance]].
cards.answer: MTD, RTO, and RPO are important planning horizons and estimates that are strongly linked to an organization's risk tolerance.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: planning horizons, strongly linked, to the risk tolerance.

cards.question: “How far back did we lose data?” Which duration answers this question?
cards.answer: The RPO
cards.explanation: The RPO looks backward, toward the last backup. The RTO looks forward, toward the restart.

cards.question: RPO, RTO, or MTD? Sort each sentence.
cards.answer: RPO: the data lost since the last backup, counted before the incident. RTO: the planned time to get running again, less than or equal to the MTD. MTD: the limit before the company is threatened, the longest tolerable downtime.
cards.explanation: RPO = data lost (before). RTO = time to restart (after). MTD = survival limit (after).

items.text: The data lost since the last backup
Counted before the incident, looking backward
The planned time to get the system running again
Must be less than or equal to the MTD
The limit before the company is threatened
The longest tolerable downtime

cards.question: “How long to restart?” Which duration answers this question?
cards.answer: The RTO
cards.explanation: The RTO is the planned time to start again. The MTD is the limit that must not be passed.

cards.question: Why are the RPO and the RTO not the same duration?
cards.answer: The RPO looks backward: how much data we accept to lose. The RTO looks forward: how long it takes to start again.
cards.explanation: A company can restart fast after losing a lot of data, or the opposite.
cards.explanation_more: Outside the manual: people sometimes talk about a fourth stopwatch, the WRT (work recovery time). It is the time to check that everything works after the restart. In this logic, the MTD equals the RTO plus the WRT.

cards.question: A company loses three hours of data and takes five hours to restart. Its survival limit is four hours. What happens?
options: The restart (5 h) goes past the survival limit (4 h)
The data loss (3 h) goes past the survival limit (4 h)
The 3 h and the 5 h add up to pass the limit
All is well, because 3 h is less than 4 h
options_why: Three hours is less than four hours. And the data loss is compared with the RPO, not with the survival limit.
The data loss is another counter: we do not add it to the downtime.
The downtime counts: five hours is longer than four.
cards.answer: The restart (5 h) goes past the survival limit (4 h)
cards.explanation: The restart time (RTO) must stay under the survival limit (MTD). Here, five hours is more than four hours.

cards.question: Put the moments on the timeline, from left to right.
cards.answer: 1 Last backup. 2 Incident. 3 System restarted (end of the RTO). 4 Serious damage (the MTD is passed).
cards.explanation: The data loss (RPO) is before the incident. The restart (RTO) comes after, before the limit (MTD).
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, figure 1.4: relation between MTD, RTO, and RPO.

items: Serious damage: the MTD is passed

cards.question: The RPO measures data loss, the RTO measures [[recovery]] time, and the [[MTD]] measures the survival limit.
cards.answer: The RPO measures data loss, the RTO measures recovery time, and the MTD measures the survival limit.
cards.explanation: Three abbreviations, three questions: how much lost, how long to restart, how long we can wait.

cards.question: What if a company sets an MTD but forgets to set an RTO?
cards.answer: It knows its limit, but nobody knows how fast it must restart. Without an RTO, the recovery is not prepared.
cards.explanation: The MTD says where the wall is. The RTO says how fast to run to avoid touching it.

cards.question: “How long can the company survive without this function?” Which duration answers?
cards.answer: The MTD
cards.explanation: The company's survival is the subject of the MTD. The RPO is about lost data.

cards.question: What does the manual say about respecting these thresholds during a real crisis?
cards.answer: Leaders adapt on the spot. These thresholds are more like guides than strict survival limits.
cards.explanation: The three durations are mostly used to plan before the crisis.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, note after figure 1.4.

concepts.name: The continuity plan: its scope and people first

paragraphes: At school, there is a fire drill. Before saving equipment or notebooks, only one thing matters: everybody gets out.
Then you plan where to meet, who warns the parents, and how to restart the lessons.
A continuity plan works the same way: people first, then ways of working, then tools. The manual says: people, processes, technologies.

decouverte.comme: First we count the students. Then we organize how lessons restart. The computers and the equipment come last.
decouverte.enVrai: In a business continuity plan (BCP), the order is fixed: people, then processes (the ways of working), then technologies. A machine can be replaced, a person cannot. The image stops here: all three are needed, and the order only says what to protect first.

decouverte.question: A fire hits a company's offices. What does the continuity plan do first of all?
decouverte.explanation: Backups and customers matter, but the first goal of a plan is the safety of people.

decouverte.titre: The plan of a chain of stores
decouverte.texte: The plan of a chain of stores covers all its stores, in every city and every country. It lists the critical functions, the threats, and the weak points. It plans the backup of data, the people in the plan, communication, and tests.

cards.question: Official definition: the order of a “BCP”
cards.answer: As with any good plan, a BCP involves people, processes, and technologies — in that order.
cards.explanation: Think of the evacuation: we count the people first, and think about machines last.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”. Learn it word for word.

cards.question: As with any good plan, a BCP [[involves]] people, processes, and technologies — in [[that order]].
cards.answer: As with any good plan, a BCP involves people, processes, and technologies — in that order.
cards.explanation: The order matters: it says what to protect first.

cards.question: As with any good plan, a BCP involves [[people]], [[processes]], and [[technologies]] — in that order.
cards.answer: As with any good plan, a BCP involves people, processes, and technologies — in that order.
cards.explanation: The three words in order: people, processes, technologies.

cards.question: Write from memory the sentence of the manual about what a BCP involves, and in what order (in English).
cards.answer: As with any good plan, a BCP involves people, processes, and technologies — in that order.
cards.explanation: A short sentence to remember as it is, with the three words in order.

cards.question: Official definition: “the BCP itself”
cards.answer: The BCP itself is the organization's commitment to maintaining the operations of the business, and the steps the organization takes to do so.
cards.explanation: The plan is a promise from the company, with the steps to keep it.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”.

cards.question: The BCP itself is [[the organization's commitment]] to [[maintaining the operations]] of the business, and [[the steps the organization takes]] to do so.
cards.answer: The BCP itself is the organization's commitment to maintaining the operations of the business, and the steps the organization takes to do so.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the commitment, maintaining the operations, and the steps to do it.

cards.question: Official definition: the scope of the “BCP”
cards.answer: The scope of the BCP must encompass all of the organization's operations, including each business area and within every geographic region that the organization does business.
cards.explanation: The scope says how far the plan goes: everything, everywhere.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”. “Encompass” means to include everything.

cards.question: The scope of the BCP must encompass [[all of the organization's operations]], including [[each business area]] and within [[every geographic region]] that the organization does business.
cards.answer: The scope of the BCP must encompass all of the organization's operations, including each business area and within every geographic region that the organization does business.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: all the operations, each business area, every region.

cards.question: Official definition: people in a continuity plan
cards.answer: People are always, without exception, your most valuable and critical asset.
cards.explanation: An asset is something of value for the company. People come before everything else.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”.

cards.question: People are [[always, without exception]], your [[most valuable]] and [[critical asset]].
cards.answer: People are always, without exception, your most valuable and critical asset.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: always without exception, the most valuable, and critical.

cards.question: Official definition: the first goal of a “BCP”
cards.answer: The first goal of any BCP must be to ensure the safety of your people during and after an emergency.
cards.explanation: Before the data and the machines: the safety of people.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”.

cards.question: The [[first goal]] of any BCP must be to [[ensure the safety of your people]] during and [[after an emergency]].
cards.answer: The first goal of any BCP must be to ensure the safety of your people during and after an emergency.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the first goal, the safety of people, and after the emergency too.

cards.question: Put the three families of the plan in the order of the manual.
cards.answer: 1 People. 2 Processes. 3 Technologies.
cards.explanation: We protect the people first, then the ways of working, then the tools.

cards.question: After the safety of people, what must we give them?
cards.answer: The resources to keep working almost normally, like shelter (another place to work) and food.
cards.explanation: People who are safe must also be able to do their work.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section on people in the BCP.

cards.question: Which people does the word “people” mean in a continuity plan?
options: Anyone the event can affect, like customers
Only the employees who have a contract with the company
Only the technical team in charge of recovery
Only the managers who make the decisions
options_why: The manual also lists contractors, customers, and vendors.
The technical team is only a small part of the people concerned.
Managers are only a part of the people concerned.
cards.answer: Anyone the event can affect, like customers
cards.explanation: The manual includes employees, contractors, customers, suppliers, and any other person affected.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: “employees, contractors, customers, vendors, and any other living human being”.

cards.question: Why does the plan put people before technologies?
cards.answer: A destroyed computer can be replaced. An injured person cannot be replaced, and without people nothing restarts.
cards.explanation: Machines are useful only if healthy people make them run.

cards.question: The plan covers each business area and each [[region]] where the company works.
cards.answer: The plan covers each business area and each region where the company works.
cards.explanation: A region that is not covered would be a hole in the plan.

cards.question: Why plan several ways to warn people during a disaster?
cards.answer: If one way fails during the disaster, another must work. If not, important people would not be warned.
cards.explanation: A single communication channel is a weak point.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: several communication methods to warn the key staff.

cards.question: What if the plan covered only one country, while the company works in three countries?
cards.answer: The other two countries would stay without protection. The manual wants the plan to cover every region where the company works.
cards.explanation: The scope of the plan must be as wide as the company.

cards.question: During a disaster, management says: “We will keep you informed only at the end.” What does the manual say about this?
options: Key managers must receive regular news
Silence avoids creating confusion during the crisis
Only the IT department needs news
News is useful only when the disaster is over
options_why: Without news, managers cannot make good decisions.
All the people responsible for the plan need to be informed, not only IT.
Decisions are made during the disaster, so news is useful right away.
cards.answer: Key managers must receive regular news
cards.explanation: Regular updates allow well-informed decisions.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: “management and key BCP stakeholders must receive regular status updates”.

cards.question: In which family of the plan does each item belong?
cards.answer: People: warn the employees, plan a shelter. Processes: supply of materials, choice of where to process data. Technologies: backups, two internet providers.
cards.explanation: People are the humans. Processes are the ways of working. Technologies are the systems.

items.text: Warn the employees that a disaster is happening
Plan a shelter for the employees
Make sure supplies keep arriving
Choose where to continue processing the critical data
Make backups of the systems and the data
Rent two internet providers

concepts.name: The processes and technologies of the plan (backup sites, backups, redundancy)

decouverte.titre: The school that moves for a week
paragraphes: A storm floods the rooms of your school. Lessons cannot stop for several weeks.
The town hall lends its big hall. The grade books exist in two copies: one at the school, one at the town hall.
Three things saved the school: another place, copies of the documents, and backup suppliers. This is what a continuity plan prepares.

decouverte.comme: You keep a spare set of keys with a neighbor. If you lose yours, you can still get in. But if the spare set is inside your own house, it is useless when the house burns.
decouverte.enVrai: A backup is a copy of the data. To be useful, it must be kept away from the main site (offsite). In the cloud, we keep copies in several regions. A region is a place in the world where data centers are. The image stops here: a company keeps several copies, not just one.

decouverte.question: A company keeps its backup copies in the room next to its server. A fire destroys the building. What happens to the copies?
options: They survive, because they are copies
They are protected by the firefighters
decouverte.explanation: A copy kept in the same place suffers the same disaster. This is why the manual asks for copies away from the site.

decouverte.texte: A company rents two internet service providers (ISP, the company that supplies its internet), several electricity suppliers, and two banks. If one fails, another takes over. This doubling of the means is called redundancy.

cards.question: Official definition: one of the essential processes of a “BCP”
cards.answer: One of the most essential BCP processes assures an organization that its critical data processing facilities and capabilities remain operational during a disaster.
cards.explanation: The critical data must keep being processed, even when the main site is hit.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Identify, Analyze, and Prioritize Business Continuity Requirements”.

cards.question: One of the most essential BCP processes assures an organization that its [[critical data processing facilities]] and [[capabilities remain operational]] during [[a disaster]].
cards.answer: One of the most essential BCP processes assures an organization that its critical data processing facilities and capabilities remain operational during a disaster.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the critical processing facilities, which remain operational, during a disaster.

cards.question: Official definition: the types of backup sites
cards.answer: The primary recover site types are hot sites, cold sites, and warm sites.
cards.explanation: Three words to remember: hot, cold, warm.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1. The manual gives details about these sites in chapter 7. Outside the manual, to help you: a hot site is ready to use right away, a cold site is an empty room, a warm site is in between.

cards.question: The primary recover site types are [[hot sites]], [[cold sites]], and [[warm sites]].
cards.answer: The primary recover site types are hot sites, cold sites, and warm sites.
cards.explanation: Hot, cold, warm: three levels of preparation of the backup place.

cards.question: Does a backup copy kept in the same building as the server protect against a fire in the building?
cards.answer: No
cards.explanation: The disaster destroys both at the same time. You need a copy somewhere else.

cards.question: A company stores its data in the cloud. What does the manual recommend?
options: Keep copies in several regions of the cloud
Keep a single copy, in the cheapest region
Copy nothing: the cloud never fails
Keep the copies only in the same data center
options_why: A single region is a weak point: a disaster there would lose the data.
The cloud can fail too. You need copies.
If the data center is hit, the original and the copies disappear together.
cards.answer: Keep copies in several regions of the cloud
cards.explanation: With several regions, the data can be recovered at any time.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Technologies”.

cards.question: Where must at least one set of backups be kept, for a company that has its own data center?
cards.answer: Away from the main site: at least one copy far from the site, in case a disaster destroys it.
cards.explanation: A copy kept outside survives the disaster that hits the site.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: “one set of your backups must be stored offsite”.

cards.question: Why does a company rent two internet service providers?
cards.answer: If one fails, the other keeps the company connected. The disaster can come from the provider, not only from the company itself.
cards.explanation: A single provider would be a weak point that everything depends on.

cards.question: Which method does the manual mention to keep the processing of critical data running during a disaster?
cards.answer: Plan the use of alternate sites during a disaster.
cards.explanation: An alternate site is another place where the business can continue.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Processes”.

cards.question: What if a company has only one electricity supplier and it fails?
cards.answer: Everything stops, even if the computers and the backups are fine. Redundancy prevents a single supplier from stopping the whole business.
cards.explanation: The manual asks for doubled supplies: electricity, water, telecommunications, and network.

cards.question: Backup or redundancy? Sort each example.
cards.answer: Backup: a copy away from the site, copies in several cloud regions, a daily copy of the files. Redundancy: two internet providers, two banks, several electricity suppliers.
cards.explanation: A backup copies the data. Redundancy doubles the means the company depends on.

items.text: A copy of the data kept away from the site
Copies in several cloud regions
A copy of the files made every day
Two internet service providers
Two banks
Several electricity suppliers

cards.question: Backups are the most [[proven]] solution against hardware and [[software]] failures.
cards.answer: Backups are the most proven solution against hardware and software failures.
cards.explanation: A technology failure is part of normal life: it is better to have copies.

cards.question: Name three things a company can do to resist a hardware failure, according to the manual.
cards.answer: Make full backups of the systems and the data. Keep at least one copy away from the site. Have redundant systems: electricity, water, telecommunications, network.
cards.explanation: Back up, move one copy away, double the means.

cards.question: A storm cuts the electricity of the server building. The company keeps working thanks to a second supplier. Which principle did it apply?
options_why: An offsite backup protects the data, not the electrical power.
Encryption (scrambling data so only the right people can read it) protects secrecy, not the continuity of power.
Least privilege (giving people only the access they need) limits what people can reach, not the power supply.
cards.answer: Redundancy
cards.explanation: A second supplier doubles the means the company depends on.
